additional_requirements: Functioning is not markedly impaired apart from the impact of the delusion(s) or its ramifications

S019.name: Delusions
S019.description: Fixed beliefs that do not change easily, even in the face of contradictory evidence.

subtypes.Persecutory Delusions: The false belief that one is being harmed or monitored by other people or organizations.
subtypes.Referential Delusions: The conviction that ordinary events, remarks, or behaviors have specific relevance to oneself.
subtypes.Grandiose Delusions: The false belief that one possesses special abilities, power, or fame.
subtypes.Erotomanic Delusions: The false belief that another person is in love with or has affection for them.
subtypes.Nihilistic Delusions: A destructive or negative conviction that the world is ending or that a major catastrophe will occur.
subtypes.Somatic Delusions: The baseless conviction that there is a serious abnormality with one's body or organs.
subtypes.Jealous Delusions: The conviction that one's spouse or romantic partner is being unfaithful without sufficient evidence.

symptom.disease_info: Delusional disorder is characterized by the presence of one or more non-bizarre or plausible-sounding delusions lasting at least one month, in the relative absence of other psychotic features such as prominent hallucinations, disorganized speech, or marked negative symptoms. Outside of the delusional beliefs, cognitive functioning and behavior are often largely preserved, and overall functioning may remain relatively intact compared with schizophrenia. The content of the delusions can be persecutory, somatic, grandiose, jealous, or erotomanic, and individuals often come to clinical attention because of interpersonal conflict, occupational problems, or legal/organizational involvement stemming from their fixed beliefs. The course tends to be chronic, with limited insight and resistance to contrary evidence, distinguishing it from overvalued ideas or mood-congruent beliefs seen in major mood disorders.

patient.stressor: About a year before presentation, Barrington was assigned to lead a high-visibility safety compliance initiative after a minor collision on one of the county bus routes drew local media scrutiny. Around that time, a contentious interaction with a senior driver—who openly questioned his authority in front of others—seemed to linger with him, and he began poring obsessively over inspection logs and incident reports, convinced that someone within the department was deliberately undermining his work. Over the following months, his belief that a small group of colleagues and outside contractors were secretly targeting his inspections hardened, leading him to stay late documenting minor issues, confront supervisors about perceived plots, and avoid certain routes and drivers when organizing trainings, even though his basic job performance remained technically adequate. The situation came to clinical attention when his supervisor, concerned about increasingly tense staff meetings and reports from church friends that he was "taking work way too personally," referred him to the employee assistance program, where his fixed, highly elaborated belief about being sabotaged became apparent.
patient.chief_complaint: “I’m here because no matter what anyone says, I know some people at work are secretly working together to set me up, and nobody seems to take that seriously.”

S019.name: Delusions
S019.description: Fixed beliefs that do not change easily, even in the face of contradictory evidence.
S019.manifestation: Ever since that driver tried to show me up in front of everyone, I’ve been completely sure that a few of the drivers and one of the outside maintenance guys are coordinating little “mistakes” and leaving things off the paperwork on purpose so that when something finally goes wrong, it’ll look like I signed off on a bad bus and they can pin it all on me, no matter how many times my boss says it’s just coincidence.
